title: Mohist Inclusive Care — concern without favoritism
when: Mozi probably flourished in the middle to late fifth century BCE, in the early Warring States era; the Mozi is an anonymous, layered collection whose chapters developed from the fifth through third centuries BCE.
people: Mo Di (Mozi) and later Mohist followers; the Confucian critics Mencius and Xunzi.
origin: Ancient China, in the competing philosophical schools of the Warring States period.
idea: Mohist inclusive care (jian’ai) asks people to extend concern across the boundaries of family, associates, and strangers. It is often rendered “universal love,” but that can mislead: Mohist texts connect an impartial attitude of care with practical efforts to benefit those with whom one interacts, not necessarily identical treatment or self-erasure. The doctrine belongs to a broader program that judged conduct and policy by whether they advanced the welfare of “all under Heaven.” Mohists argued that partiality fuels conflict: rulers privilege their own states, families their own interests, and individuals themselves, making injury to outsiders seem acceptable. Their alternative links moral concern to reciprocal benefit and condemns aggressive war as a grave instance of pursuing advantage at others’ expense. The surviving Mozi is not a single author’s treatise; its arguments and formulations reflect a movement that grew and changed over generations.
relevance: Inclusive care offers a sharp test for modern ethics and public policy: whose welfare counts when decisions cross borders, communities, or generations? It challenges favoritism while raising live questions about whether impartial concern can coexist with special obligations to loved ones.
